situation:
You are the finance manager at THORNWOOD VALLEY HEALTH SYSTEM, a nonprofit hospital system with three hospitals and a network of outpatient clinics. The vice president of finance (judge) arrived a year ago to lead a turnaround after two years of losses and has asked you to recommend whether the system should hand its gift shops and outpatient pharmacy counters to an outside operator.

The system has run those shops and counters itself for decades, staffing them with its own employees and buying its own merchandise. A national retail operator has offered to take them over for a flat fee per site, turning payroll and inventory carrying cost into one predictable charge and removing fixed cost the turnaround plan has to find somewhere.

The transaction records point one way. Sales per square foot at the operator's other hospital sites run well ahead of the system's own, and its merchandising is the reason: tighter product ranges and displays built around what patients' families buy. The shop staff read the same records differently, and say the counts miss the prescriptions they hold for patients who cannot pay that day.

Handing the shops and counters to the national retail operator removes the fixed payroll and inventory cost the turnaround needs, and it costs the system the staff who hold prescriptions for patients who cannot pay that day, along with part of the charitable care figure its public annual report has carried for years. Keeping the shops in house and cutting fixed cost by trimming hours and merchandise range instead protects that practice and that figure, and it costs the turnaround most of the savings, leaving the plan short of what the board was promised.

The vice president of finance (judge) has asked you to explain what the sales and transaction records can be used for beyond billing, explain what financial-information management covers across a system this size, explain where ethics enters a decision read from data the staff dispute, discuss what the system must report publicly, and explain why merchandising matters to a retail operation.

The vice president of finance (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas. After you have presented and answered the questions, the vice president of finance (judge) will thank you for your work.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the vice president of finance (judge) of THORNWOOD VALLEY HEALTH SYSTEM. Business background is the same as the situation above.

You arrived a year ago to lead the turnaround after two years of losses, and the board is watching. You want the finance manager to explain what the sales and transaction records can be used for beyond billing, explain what financial-information management covers across a system this size, explain where ethics enters a decision read from data the shop staff dispute, discuss what the system must report publicly, explain why merchandising matters to a retail operation, and tell you plainly whether to hand the shops and counters to the national retail operator or keep them in house.

After the finance manager has presented, you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: Two years on, what does this change about the shops?
What might we only notice long after the change is made?
